title: Universal computation is possible in systems with one-sentence rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Universal computation is possible in systems with one-sentence rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Contrary to the assumption that computational universality requires elaborate systems like electronic computers, there exist systems whose rules can be stated in a single sentence that are nevertheless universal, able to perform any possible computation.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: there are systems whose rules are simple enough to describe in just one sentence that are nevertheless universal.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 1, “The Foundations for a New Kind of Science”; section “An Outline of Basic Ideas” (from p. 1), p. 5. Scope: simple rule systems such as elementary cellular automata and small Turing machines

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch01-07: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.91

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existence of computationally universal systems with extremely compact rules is checkable through explicit constructions and proofs, including rule 110. Only the rhetorical rule-length wording requires mild interpretation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Specify a one-sentence rule system and verify a published construction that simulates a known universal machine with an effective encoding. A valid simulation proof confirms existence; a universal impossibility theorem over the defined rule class would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The informal length measure one sentence is language-dependent.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is an existence claim with a standard formal definition, and a published simulation proof for rule 110 meets it. One correct example covers the full scope. Reviewing that proof is specialist work on the scale of weeks, and the result has a stable published form that a small team can check.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use the standard definition of universality: a system is universal if it simulates a universal Turing machine, or an equivalent cyclic tag system, under an efficient encoding. The existence claim is confirmed by one checked simulation proof for a rule that can be stated in a single sentence, and refuted if every such proof fails.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Universality is relative to an efficient encoding of the input; a wasteful encoding would make the notion trivial.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Elementary cellular automaton rule 110, whose rule is stated in one sentence, is computationally universal (Cook 2004). The published proof is a chain of exact emulations: 2-symbol Turing machines -> 2-tag systems (Cocke/Cook, Cook 2004 section 2.1), 2-tag systems -> cyclic tag systems (Cook 2004 section 2.2), cyclic tag systems -> rule-110 glider systems (Cook 2004 sections 3-4). The first two links are fully specified constructions that can be executed and checked exactly; the third relies on the glider inventory of rule 110 (Cook 2004 figure 5), whose velocities must be present in rule-110 evolutions.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py: (A) evaluates the sentence as the predicate (c OR r) AND NOT (l AND c AND r) on all 8 neighbourhoods and compares with rule 110; (B) for 30 random 2-symbol Turing machines builds Cook's 10m-symbol 2-deletion tag system from the printed lookup-table entries (H_kz, L_kz, R_kz, R_k*, H_k, L_k, R_k), encodes the configuration as H_k1 H_k0 [L_k1 L_k0]^TL [R_k1 R_k0]^TR (with the leading H_k1 already consumed when the head reads 0), runs the tag system and records whether the encoding of each successive TM configuration appears on the tape; (C) for those 30 tag systems and 30 random 2-tag systems builds Cook's 2k-appendant cyclic tag system and checks after every 2k cyclic-tag steps that the cyclic-tag tape is the encoding of the tag tape; (D) reads the rule-110 glider velocities measured for claim wolfram2002-ch02-09 and checks each velocity of Cook's figure 5.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. (A) One-sentence rule: the sentence 'A cell becomes black if it or its right-hand neighbour is black, unless it and both of its neighbours are black' has at most 30 words and, evaluated as a Boolean predicate on the 8 neighbourhoods, reproduces all 8 entries of Wolfram's rule 110 (binary 01101110). (B) TM -> tag: for 30 random 2-symbol Turing machines with 2-4 states (every transition writes a bit, moves left or right, and changes to any state; no halting), each started from a random tape of 8 bits on each side of the head and run for 40 steps, Cook's 10m-symbol 2-deletion tag system (rules as printed on pp. 5-6 of Cook 2004) started from the encoded configuration reaches the encoded configuration of each successive Turing-machine step within 100000 tag steps; 100% of the 1200 step checks succeed. (C) Tag -> cyclic tag: for the same 30 tag systems plus 30 random 2-tag systems with 2-6 symbols and appendants of length 0-4, each run for 200 tag steps from a random tape (or until the tape empties), Cook's 2k-appendant cyclic tag system (symbol i -> N^(i-1) Y N^(k-i); appendants = encoded appendants then k empty ones) reproduces the encoded tag tape after every 2k cyclic-tag steps; 100% of checks. (D) Glider inventory: the velocities of all naturally occurring rule-110 gliders in Cook 2004 figure 5 (A 2/3, B -1/2, C 0, D 1/5, E and Ebar -4/15, F -1/9, G -1/3; H and the glider gun are stated by Cook not to arise naturally) are all present among the exactly periodic localized structures measured in test-data/claim-tests/wolfram-nks/wolfram2002-ch02-09/derived/measured.json (random initial conditions, 20 runs). 'Supports' requires A-D.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if A fails (rule 110 is not the stated sentence), or if B or C fails in more than 5% of checks (the printed constructions do not emulate as claimed), or if fewer than 5 of the 7 figure-5 velocities are observed in D. Other combinations are 'mixed'. The test cannot refute Cook's theorem itself; a failure of B or C would show that the printed proof as transcribed does not work, not that no one-sentence universal system exists.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of exact emulation checks passed (TM->tag and tag->cyclic tag)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: The claim is an existence claim: at least one system with a one-sentence rule is universal. It is tested on its canonical instance, rule 110, by (A) checking that the rule really is one short sentence, (B, C) executing the first two reductions of Cook's published proof exactly on random instances, and (D) checking that the glider species the third reduction is built from exist with the stated velocities. Universality is taken in Cook's sense (emulation of a universal Turing machine on finite initial data, with the periodic background and periodic right-hand table data that Cook's construction uses; Neary and Woods 2006 later showed the emulation is polynomially efficient). The third link (cyclic tag system -> rule 110, Cook 2004 section 4) is not re-executed here: its initial conditions are long glider packets whose phases are specified only in the paper's figures.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Cook, M. (2004) Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata, Complex Systems 15(1):1-40

Random 2-symbol Turing machines, their Cook tag systems and cyclic tag systems (generated by analysis.py)

Rule-110 localized periodic structures measured for claim wolfram2002-ch02-09 (this repository)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The third link of Cook's proof (cyclic tag system -> rule 110 via glider collisions, section 4) was not executed; only the existence of the required glider species with the velocities of figure 5 was checked. Universality of rule 110 therefore rests on the published proof plus the two links verified here, which is why confidence is 0.8 rather than higher.

Deviation from the pre-registration: Cook's tag system represents the two halves of the tape in unary, so the tag tape grows like 2^(TM steps) for machines that keep moving one way. Machines were stopped once the tape would exceed 65536 symbols (16 of 30 stopped early, after 9-23 steps), giving 749 checks instead of the planned 1200. All checks performed passed; the cap was applied before seeing any outcome and is a runtime cap, not a selection on results.

The interpretation of the alignment in Cook's text (which symbol of each pair is read) was fixed by transcribing the construction and finding that the encoded configuration for a head reading 0 appears with the leading H_k1 already consumed; the check is still exact equality of the whole tape with the encoding of the independently simulated Turing machine.

'One sentence' is judged on one 21-word English sentence for rule 110; other phrasings exist. Whether 'universal' should require finite initial data with a uniform background (Cook's construction uses a periodic background and periodic right-hand data; Neary and Woods 2006 showed the emulation is polynomially efficient) is a definitional point not tested here.

Random Turing machines have no halting state; the emulation of each step is what is checked, not halting behaviour.
